title: Lemony Snicket's A Series of Unfortunate Events
full_review:
The delightfully macabre "Lemony Snicket's A Series of Unfortunate Events" (Paramount) joins the rest of the season's children's films that adults can enjoy every bit as much as the tykes.

Based on the books "The Bad Beginning," "The Reptile Room" and "The Wide Window" by Lemony Snicket (aka Daniel Handler), director Brad Silberling's widescreen adaptation gives Jim Carrey a field day embodying various characters with his customary aplomb.

At the center of the story are the three Baudelaire children -- Violet (Emily Browning), the 14-year-old inventor; 12-year-old Klaus (Liam Aiken), the book lover; and Sunny (Kara and Shelby Hoffman), the infant with a precocious knack for biting anything and everything.

After their parents perish in a mysterious fire which destroys their large mansion, the three waifs are taken by the thick-headed solicitor, Mr. Poe (Timothy Spall), to live with the evil Count Olaf (Carrey), a hammy and transparently villainous character who cares only for the Baudelaires' fortune.

He puts them to work scrubbing the floors and making dinner for him and his creepy actor friends, and later tries to kill them by locking them in a car on train tracks. He fails in that wicked plot, and the children are transferred first to the care of a kindly but eccentric reptile keeper, Uncle Monty (Billy Connolly), a herpetologist who keeps a "deadly" viper that turns out to be as meek as a pussycat, and then to dotty Aunt Josephine (Meryl Streep), who harbors a serious phobia about real estate agents.

All of this is narrated in droll fashion by the ubiquitous Jude Law, seen only in silhouette here. Just when matters threaten to get too scary or intense, the action stops, and we see Snicket at the typewriter, figuring out what happens next. This device helps keep the film from getting too intense for youngsters. There's also the reassuring sense throughout that nothing too terrible is really going to happen to the children.

Carrey is a marvel as the dastardly Olaf, the perfect storybook villain, rather like mean Uncle Barnaby in Laurel and Hardy's "March of the Wooden Soldiers," and his impersonations of a weaselly lab assistant and an old sea captain in pursuit of the orphans are priceless.

Streep is a daffy loon, proving again how very fine she can be in comedy. Connolly is endearingly sympathetic. The children are perfect, right down to the Hoffman twins as the gurgling Sunny.

Rick Heinrichs' production design -- Boston, by way of Charles Dickens and J.K. Rowling, with some dollops of Edward Gorey -- is simply splendid.

The film has an excellent moral ending which wraps things up on a high note. And special mention should be made of the clever Gorey-like closing credits, which extend the fun to the very last frame.

This film contains some mildly intense situations and a smattering of crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
